clue.text: In back room, rare vodka highball served thus?

indicators.note: back says the hidden letters are read backwards
In says the letters sit inside the words that follow, room, rare vodka

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A drinker in a back room orders a highball of vodka and wonders how it should be served.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft leaves 'In' as a link; it is the signal for the hidden run, so it is marked as the indicator. A highball is a cricket ball bowled high, not a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowler who delivers a high ball does so with the arm swung over the shoulder, a cricket term.

clue.text: Edison contrived a legal position for play

indicators.note: contrived means put together artificially, so the letters of Edison are rearranged

explanation.surface: Thomas Edison invents a loophole that makes some play legal.
explanation.definitionFit: In football, rugby and hockey a player in a legitimate position to receive or play the ball is said to be in this state.

clue.text: 13 following Hendrix, an apology for manly affection?

definitions.meaning: 13 down names a misheard song lyric; this is the famous mishearing of Jimi Hendrix's line from Purple Haze, 'kiss the sky'
read literally, the phrase is a polite request for pardon from a man about to kiss another man

explanation.surface: Someone apologises after Jimi Hendrix for showing one man's affection.
explanation.walkthrough: Hendrix sang 'Excuse me while I kiss the sky' in Purple Haze; many listeners famously heard 'this guy', and he sometimes played along on stage.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the best-known misheard lyric of a Hendrix song, and literally it begs pardon before a kiss between men.

clue.text: Doubtful this could make Carol happy

indicators.note: could make says these letters can be rebuilt into another word, so Carol happy is rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is unsure whether a gift will please a woman named Carol.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the other way round: the answer, rearranged, could make CAROL HAPPY, with 'this' standing for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An apocryphal story is of dubious authenticity, widely told but probably untrue.

clue.text: See 26
Stay after passport centre makes a bit of a mess

indicators.note: after puts the stay piece behind the passport piece
the centre of passport is its middle two letters, picked out from the word

parts.note: to stay somewhere temporarily is to lodge there

explanation.surface: A traveller's long stay leaves a smudge in the middle of the passport.
explanation.definitionFit: A splodge is a blot or smear, a small patch of mess.

clue.text: Support an old Sodomite's offering early in auction

parts.note: to second a motion is to support it
Lot was the biblical resident of Sodom who fled before its destruction; the 's is a link meaning has

explanation.surface: An ancient citizen of Sodom backs an item put up for sale at auction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sodomite' here means simply an inhabitant of Sodom, the biblical city.
explanation.definitionFit: Items at auction are sold in numbered order, so the item numbered two comes up near the start.

clue.text: Legendary demon upset one who reportedly perished with the 26 4

definitions.text: one who reportedly perished with the 26 4

indicators.note: upset means knocked over or thrown into disorder, so the letters of Legendary demon are rearranged

explanation.surface: A mythical demon is overturned by a person said to have died beside a murdered nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: The ballad 'The Bonnie Earl o' Moray' has 'They have slain the Earl o' Moray, and laid him on the green'; a listener misheard the last words as a second victim, giving the term for misheard lyrics.
explanation.definitionFit: The ballad seemed to say an imagined woman was killed alongside the Scottish earl, though she never existed, hence 'reportedly'.

clue.text: Dared to drop a clue for eg 'exhume something unpleasant'

indicators.note: to drop tells us the following letter is let fall from the word Dared

parts.note: the letters GE with UP make a clue for eg, since GE written upwards in a down light reads EG

explanation.surface: A setter dared to drop in a clue defining a word for digging up something nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to drop' takes A out of Dared. The second piece is itself a little reverse clue: GE going up in a down entry reads EG.
explanation.definitionFit: To dredge up is to bring an unpleasant past matter back into view, like exhuming a buried body.

clue.text: Trying volatile gases to suppress the female principle

indicators.note: to suppress is to hold down, so the gases piece wraps around and contains the female principle piece
volatile means unstable and changeable, so the letters of gases are rearranged

parts.note: in Chinese philosophy yin is the passive female principle, paired with yang

explanation.surface: A chemist attempts to keep unstable gases from swamping the feminine force.
explanation.definitionFit: To essay something is to attempt it, so essaying means attempting.

clue.text: This way acceptable to back sadistic pervert

parts.note: sic is Latin for thus, so, in this way

indicators.note: to back means to go in reverse, so the acceptable piece is read backwards

parts.note: OK means acceptable

explanation.surface: Someone asks if it's fine to support a cruel deviant in this manner.
explanation.definitionFit: A sicko is slang for a person with sick, perverted or sadistic tastes.

clue.text: Deck tours guided by Meat Loaf, Cher, Jagger and Bowie?

definitions.text: Meat Loaf, Cher, Jagger and Bowie?

indicators.note: guided means steered around, so the letters of Deck tours are rearranged

explanation.surface: Four stars of rock lead guided tours of a ship's deck.
explanation.walkthrough: Meat Loaf sang 'Dead Ringer for Love' with Cher, and Jagger and Bowie recorded 'Dancing in the Street' together; the question mark marks definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Both pairs of singers recorded famous songs together, making them examples of two-voice rock recordings.

clue.text: Wrecking old city besieged by poor design

indicators.note: besieged by means surrounded by, so the design letters go around the old city
poor means badly made, so the letters of design are rearranged

parts.note: Troy is the ancient city besieged by the Greeks

explanation.surface: An ancient city is ruined by a badly planned siege.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor' looks like a judgement on the design but is the anagram signal; 'besieged by' puts the old city inside the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To wreck something is to ruin it completely, a synonym of demolishing it.

clue.text: See 2
See 6
It's essential to back newspaper feature after plan is redrafted

indicators.note: after puts the newspaper feature behind the rearranged letters
redrafted means written out again in a new form, so the letters of plan is are rearranged

parts.note: a column is a regular article in a newspaper

explanation.surface: An editor insists a newspaper must support a regular feature once the layout is revised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to back' looks like 'to support', but means 'to the back' as a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: The backbone runs down the back and is vital to its structure, so it is essential to that part of the body.

clue.text: With which one is naked and free

definitions.meaning: someone wearing no clothes at all is dressed in no garments
free means having no engagements, an empty diary

explanation.surface: Being nude is a kind of liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: Having no clothes on means being naked, and having no plans on means being available.

clue.text: See 2
See 2
Adieu, extinct bats! There's something wrong

indicators.note: bats is slang for crazy, so the letters of Adieu, extinct are scrambled

explanation.surface: A farewell to bat species now extinct, with a sense that something is amiss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bats' looks like the animals but is the adjective for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Inexactitude is inaccuracy, a mistake or error; Churchill's 'terminological inexactitude' meant a lie.

clue.text: Your mate regularly seen chasing silver markets

indicators.note: chasing means following behind, so the regular letters come after the silver

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter is taken from Your mate

explanation.surface: A friend is often spotted pursuing silver at the markets.
explanation.definitionFit: An agora was a marketplace and public square in ancient Greece; these are its plural.

clue.text: Folly of designer cut when cold outside

indicators.note: outside says the cold piece goes around the shortened designer

parts.note: icy means very cold

indicators.note: cut says the designer's name loses its final letter

parts.note: Christian Dior was a French fashion designer

explanation.surface: A fashion designer's foolish cut when the weather outside is freezing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' looks like a tailor's cut but means the designer's name loses its last letter; 'outside' puts the cold around what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: Folly and idiocy are both synonyms for foolishness or stupid behaviour.

clue.text: Note abbreviated sense of humour

definitions.meaning: the fifth degree of the scale in tonic sol-fa
the initials used in personal ads for a sense of humour

explanation.surface: A short message mentions someone's sense of humour.
explanation.definitionFit: In tonic sol-fa the fifth scale degree is this syllable, and lonely-hearts adverts use the same initials for wit.

clue.text: Signed off, old and detached

indicators.note: off means wrong or not right, so the letters of Signed are rearranged

parts.note: aged means old

explanation.surface: An elderly person signs off and becomes withdrawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Signed off' looks like a phrase, but 'off' is the anagram signal on SIGNED.
explanation.definitionFit: Disengaged means separated or not involved, the same as detached.

clue.text: Country messing with one genotype?

indicators.note: messing with means jumbling up, so the answer and the letters of one together rearrange to make genotype

explanation.surface: A nation tampers with someone's genetic makeup.
explanation.walkthrough: Read it backwards: the country, jumbled together with ONE, gives GENOTYPE.
explanation.definitionFit: Egypt is a nation in north-east Africa, an example of a country.

clue.text: Do not hit girl!

definitions.meaning: to fail to strike a target
a young unmarried woman, as in a title

explanation.surface: A stern order not to strike a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: To fail to hit a target is to miss it, and a young woman is addressed with the same title.

clue.text: How a lady starts getting excited, with hesitation

indicators.note: starts means the opening letter of each of How, a and lady

parts.note: feeling tingly is having a thrill of excitement

explanation.surface: A woman begins to get thrilled, but hesitantly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How' is not a question word here; its first letter starts the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something haltingly means doing it with pauses and stops, hesitantly.

clue.text: In advance, securing room to manoeuvre a murder victim

indicators.note: securing means holding fast, so the early piece encloses the rearranged letters

parts.note: early means ahead of time

indicators.note: to manoeuvre is to move around, so the letters of room and a are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone books a room ahead of time in which to move about, then finds a body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to manoeuvre' rearranges room plus A, and 'securing' holds them inside 'in advance'. The victim is the earl of the Scottish ballad.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish ballad 'The Bonnie Earl o' Moray' laments the nobleman's killing in 1592.

clue.text: Don's trip with boy

definitions.note: read as the verb dons, puts on clothing, rather than a possessive

parts.note: a slip is a trip or stumble
a son is a boy child

explanation.surface: A university lecturer's journey with a lad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don's' looks like a possessive of an Oxford don, but is the verb: dons.
explanation.definitionFit: To don a garment is to put it on quickly, just as one pulls it over oneself easily.

clue.text: Hides from this attempt to imprison queen

indicators.note: to imprison is to lock inside, so the attempt piece goes around the queen

parts.note: a try is an attempt
Anne was Queen of Great Britain from 1702 to 1714

explanation.surface: Someone takes cover from an effort to jail the queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hides' looks like a verb of concealment, but is the noun: animal skins.
explanation.definitionFit: Animal skins are turned into leather at a works, so skins come from it as leather.
